analysis.one_liner: Bans members of Congress and their families from betting on political outcomes via prediction markets.
analysis.headline: A House committee advanced the bill on a 5–4 vote in June 2026, but the full House has not voted on it.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar members of Congress, their spouses, and their dependent children from placing bets on prediction markets — platforms where people wager real money on whether a government policy, a government action, or a political outcome will happen. Lawmakers often learn about those decisions before the public does. Violators would owe a fee of $2,000 or 10% of the bet, whichever is greater, plus any profits, and could not pay it out of their office allowance or campaign funds.
analysis.who_benefits: The public, which gets a rule keeping lawmakers and their families from cashing in on betting markets that price government decisions they may know about before everyone else. The Treasury also collects the fees from violators, and voters get clearer lines between congressional service and personal wagering.

how_it_helps.text: Bars members of Congress, their spouses, and their dependent children from entering any bet, contract, or transaction that depends on a government policy, a government action, or a political outcome — or on any other event they learned of through congressional service.
Attaches a real price to violations: a fee of $2,000 or 10% of the transaction, whichever is greater, plus every dollar of net gain the bet produced, deposited in the Treasury.

Closes escape hatches: the fee cannot be paid from the member's official office allowance or from campaign donations, and a former member who resigns or retires without paying can be referred to the Department of Justice.
Directs the ethics offices to write interpretive guidance so members know what counts as a covered bet, and takes effect 180 days after enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and their families, who would lose the ability to trade on prediction markets and would owe fees plus profits if they violated the ban. Prediction-market platforms would lose that small slice of customers. The public pays nothing directly.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and their families

drawbacks.text: The penalty is a fee, not a fine or a crime: the minimum exposure is $2,000, which a wealthy member could treat as a cost of doing business rather than a deterrent.
The ban reaches only prediction markets. A member could still trade stocks or other assets on the same inside knowledge of pending government action; this bill does not touch that.

Enforcement runs through the existing congressional ethics offices, which act 'at the direction of' discretion built into the bill; there is no independent prosecutor and no private right of action for the public.

The catch-all covering 'any other event' a member learned of through service is broad and undefined, which could make it hard for members and their families to know what ordinary transactions are allowed until guidance is issued.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a real but modest ethics rule. It targets a genuine conflict — lawmakers wagering on the very government decisions they shape or learn of early — and its fee-plus-profits structure at least claws back winnings. But the penalty is light, the scope is narrow (prediction markets only, not stocks), and enforcement depends entirely on the same ethics offices that police Congress today. It would help more than it costs; it just helps less than its title suggests.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared the House committee that handles it on a narrow 5–4 vote, but it has not reached the House floor and Congress is still in session, so it could still move or quietly die.

narrative.text: Representative Bryan Steil introduced the bill on June 18, 2026, joined by four original Republican cosponsors, and it was referred to the Committee on House Administration.
Eight more Republicans had signed on as cosponsors, for 8 total on top of the sponsor.
On June 24, 2026, the committee held a markup and ordered the bill reported with amendments by a recorded vote of 5–4 — a narrow margin that signals resistance even inside the committee.
Since that committee vote, the House has taken no further action on the bill in the provided record, and the Congress runs through January 3, 2027.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet. Until the House votes, members of Congress and their families remain free to bet on political outcomes, and the prediction-market platforms keep serving them.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor is a Republican and no Democrat has signed on, but the provided record for the 5–4 committee vote does not show how the parties split, so the shape of opposition is not confirmed.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and their families
industries.note: They would lose the ability to wager real money on government policies, government actions, and political outcomes — information members often receive before the public does — and would owe fees plus profits for violations.

industries.industry: Prediction market operators (betting platforms for political and policy events)
industries.note: They would lose a small but awkward customer base: lawmakers and their households. Their interest in keeping those customers runs against the bill's purpose of keeping inside political knowledge out of the betting pool.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has cleared committee on a narrow 5–4 vote but has no Democratic cosponsors and no recorded floor action since June. The most likely path is that it waits for a floor slot — often the suspension calendar near the end of a session, which requires a two-thirds majority — and runs out of time when the Congress ends on January 3, 2027.
